evidence_quotes.text: An LLM is an interpreter where the prompt is the static program and the question is the dynamic input.
An LLM is also a partial evaluator that can specialize code and neural network weights.

core_insights.generalization: Any component whose inputs are partially known at build time (tenant config, schema, locale, business rules) is a candidate for compile-time specialization instead of runtime interpretation.
core_insights.insight: An LLM can be modeled as an interpreter with the prompt as static program and the user question as dynamic input; as a partial evaluator it specializes code and neural-network weights on inputs known ahead of time. This reframes 'prompting' as program specialization rather than text conditioning.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Gives engineers a precise, classical-CS lens for what an agent actually does at inference time: it is not just retrieval-plus-generation, it is a specialization step where everything known at build time can be collapsed out of the runtime computation. That suggests concrete optimizations (precompute, prune, bake in constants) rather than more prompt text.

evidence_quotes.text: First projection: partially evaluating an interpreter with a program yields an executable.
Second projection: partially evaluating a partial evaluator with an interpreter yields a compiler.
Third projection: partially evaluating a partial evaluator with itself yields a compiler generator.

core_insights.generalization: For any generative pipeline, ask which 'projection' you are shipping: an artifact, a tool that produces artifacts, or a tool that produces such tools. Value and reuse increase along that ladder.
core_insights.insight: The three Futamura projections supply a tiered specialization ladder: partially evaluating an interpreter with a program yields an executable; partially evaluating the partial evaluator with an interpreter yields a compiler; partially evaluating the partial evaluator with itself yields a compiler generator. In agent terms: prompt-specialized instance, prompt-compiler, and a generator that produces prompt-compilers.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It provides a principled way to decide where specialization should live in a system — per-request, per-tenant, or per-domain — and makes explicit that the highest-leverage artifact is the generator, not any single generated program. That is an architectural boundary choice, not a prompt-tuning detail.

evidence_quotes.text: Specializing MNIST to recognize only digits 0 to 4 using partial evaluation.
Models can be drastically reduced in size and improved in accuracy without retraining by evaluating known static inputs.

core_insights.generalization: Treat the general model as an interpreter and the deployment context as static input; produce a residual specialized model per deployment target, and measure size/latency/accuracy deltas against the general model.
core_insights.insight: Specialization can be pushed into model weights, not just prompts: evaluating known static inputs into the network (demonstrated by specializing MNIST to recognize only digits 0 through 4) is claimed to shrink the model and improve accuracy without retraining.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If static-input folding at weight level works, deployment of specialized models gets cheaper and more accurate for narrow tasks — an alternative to fine-tuning and distillation for the same goal of tailoring a general model to a specific task. That changes the deployment architecture: specialization becomes a build/compile step, not a training run.

evidence_quotes.text: Partial evaluation provides a mathematically sound way to achieve recursive self-improvement.
AI will systematically optimize its own models and software infrastructure.

core_insights.generalization: Self-improvement loops are safest when framed as specialization against a fixed specification (equivalence-preserving), not as unconstrained self-modification.
core_insights.insight: Partial evaluation is proposed as a mathematically grounded route to recursive self-improvement: an AI system can specialize and optimize its own code and weights without needing complete understanding of itself.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If self-specialization is a legitimate optimization loop rather than science fiction, then harness design must include a feedback path where the system's own artifacts become static inputs to the next specialization round — with equivalence checks as the safety mechanism. That is an eval/CI architecture question.

evidence_quotes.text: Code has become free; therefore, depending on old generic software and open-source dependencies is dead.

core_insights.generalization: Any reuse decision is a buy-vs-build-vs-generate calculation that shifts whenever generation cost drops; re-run that calculation per dependency, not per project.
core_insights.insight: If code generation is cheap, the economically correct move is to generate and statically link bespoke code rather than depend on large open-source dependency trees — generic software and its reuse model become obsolete.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It inverts a decades-old supply-chain assumption: the dependency graph was a cost-saving device, and that trade now loses on cost. summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Erik Meijer
  • Channel: AI Native Dev
  • Main topic: Hyper-personalization, partial evaluation, Futumura projections, and the future of software development in the age of AI
  • Purpose: To explain why traditional software engineering practices, open-source reuse models, and IP protections are becoming obsolete in the era of AI-driven partial evaluation and weight-space programming. Erik Meijer argues that software development is shifting from generic, mass-produced code to hyper-personalized, custom-generated software. Using principles of partial evaluation and Futumura projections (the three projections of Dr. Futumura), he explains how large language models (LLMs) act as interpreters, partial evaluators, compilers, and generators, making code-writing cheap, eliminating human-written dependencies, and transforming software economics.

Topic Map

The Software Chop Shop & Hyper-Personalization

  • Explanation: Comparing software development to the automotive or fashion 'chop shop' concept, where generic software is customized or entirely regenerated for individual needs rather than relying on bloated generic applications.
  • Key claims:
    • Old software is generic apps built for a wide audience solving particular problems.
    • Users want fully personalized software tailored specifically to them.
    • Code has become free; therefore, depending on old generic software and open-source dependencies is dead.
  • Examples:
    • Using Excel or Outlook as generic tools versus generating a custom app for a specific business problem.
  • Terminology:
    • hyper-personalized software
    • software chop shop
    • generic software
  • Why it matters: It explains why building monolithic open-source libraries or depending on massive software suites is obsolete when AI can instantly generate bespoke solutions.

The Three Projections of Doctor Futumura

  • Explanation: Applying Futumura projections to AI and software, showing how an interpreter can be specialized to produce an executable, a compiler, and a compiler generator.
  • Key claims:
    • First projection: partially evaluating an interpreter with a program yields an executable.
    • Second projection: partially evaluating a partial evaluator with an interpreter yields a compiler.
    • Third projection: partially evaluating a partial evaluator with itself yields a compiler generator.
  • Examples:
    • Specializing an interpreter for n=5 to eliminate recursion and branches.
  • Terminology:
    • Futumura projections
    • partial evaluation
    • residual program
    • interpreter
    • compiler generator
  • Why it matters: It provides a rigorous theoretical foundation from computer science showing how AI models function as partial evaluators.

LLMs as Interpreters and Partial Evaluators

  • Explanation: Demonstrating that LLMs are not just chat bots, but interpreters and partial evaluators that can optimize models and code by removing static inputs and dependencies.
  • Key claims:
    • An LLM is an interpreter where the prompt is the static program and the question is the dynamic input.
    • An LLM is also a partial evaluator that can specialize code and neural network weights.
    • Partial evaluation provides a mathematically sound way to achieve recursive self-improvement.
  • Examples:
    • Specializing MNIST to recognize only digits 0 to 4 using partial evaluation.
  • Terminology:
    • LLM
    • partial evaluator
    • recursive self-improvement (RSI)
    • weight-space programming
  • Why it matters: It reframes AI capabilities in terms of classical program generation and optimization theory.

The Collapse of Software IP and Patents

  • Explanation: Analyzing how software patents and copyrights are becoming useless because code is either open mathematics or unprotectable machine instructions, and code generation makes copying irrelevant.
  • Key claims:
    • Software patents require a human inventor; copyright requires a human author.
    • Code has become free, so protecting or licensing it is pointless.
    • If your business relies on lawyers to win, you have already lost.
  • Examples:
    • Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank and Oracle v. Google cases regarding software patents and API declarations.
  • Terminology:
    • software patents
    • copyright act
    • intellectual property (IP)
    • fair use
  • Why it matters: It challenges conventional business models built around software licensing and IP enforcement.

Key Points

Code is free

  • Explanation: Because AI can generate code instantly and cheaply, the cost of writing code has dropped to zero.
  • Evidence: Comparison of the cost of generation versus monthly SaaS subscriptions.
  • Practical implication: Companies selling generic software will face severe disruption and layoffs.

Tokens scale, humans don't

  • Explanation: Human productivity does not follow Moore's Law, but AI token processing power and capabilities scale rapidly.
  • Evidence: Software engineering methodologies like Agile failed to make human coders exponentially more productive.
  • Practical implication: Organizations must replace human bottlenecks with AI-driven generation and agents.

LLMs achieve recursive self-improvement via partial evaluation

  • Explanation: Partial evaluation allows AI systems to optimize code and neural networks recursively without needing god-like understanding.
  • Evidence: Recent MIT papers on 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming'.
  • Practical implication: AI will systematically optimize its own models and software infrastructure.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Three Futumura Projections

  • How it works: Taking a partial evaluator (mix) and feeding interpreters and itself into it to derive executables, compilers, and compiler generators.
  • Components:
    • First Projection (Executable): mix(interpreter, program) -> executable
    • Second Projection (Compiler): mix(mix, interpreter) -> compiler
    • Third Projection (Generator): mix(mix, mix) -> compiler generator
  • When to use: When optimizing program execution and understanding program specialization.

Three Ways to Specialize a Model

  • How it works: Methods to adapt a general-purpose model to specific tasks.
  • Components:
    • Partial Evaluation
    • Fine-Tuning
    • Distillation
  • When to use: When tailoring large models for efficient, specialized deployment.

Examples & Case Studies

PostgreSQL 19 release delays attributed to AI finding bugs in human-written code faster than humans can ship.

  • Illustrates: Human software is full of bugs, and AI is exposing the flaws in human coding standards.
  • Lesson: Human-written software is inherently buggy; AI verification will become mandatory.

Specializing a neural network (MNIST) to recognize only digits 0 through 4.

  • Illustrates: Partial evaluation applied to neural network weights (weight-space programming).
  • Lesson: Models can be drastically reduced in size and improved in accuracy without retraining by evaluating known static inputs.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Stop relying on bloated open-source dependency trees; use AI to statically link and generate custom applications.
    • Embrace partial evaluation concepts in prompt engineering and model optimization.
  • Strategic:
    • Shift business models from selling software licenses to selling outcomes and services built with AI.
    • Prepare for recursive self-improvement in AI systems by 2027.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How will enterprise architectures adapt to zero-dependency, AI-generated micro-applications?
    • What are the legal and practical limits of weight-space programming and model distillation?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • PostgreSQL 19 is late due to AI finding bugs in human-written code (satirical/hypothetical projection for 2026). (future prediction / satire)
  • LLMs can act as partial evaluators for weight-space programming. (technical claim)

Notable Quotes

"Given enough compute, all software is solved." (at 24:59) "The safest code is code you never run." (at 15:42) "Good artists copy, great artists steal." (at 17:10) "Tokens scale, humans don't." (at 18:19) "If your business relies on lawyers to win, you already lost." (at 30:30)

Compressed Summary

  • Software is transitioning from generic and expensive to custom and cheap via AI partial evaluation.
  • Futumura projections explain how interpreters, compilers, and code generators relate mathematically.
  • LLMs act as partial evaluators, enabling weight-space programming and recursive self-improvement.
  • Software IP, patents, and copyright are increasingly irrelevant because code generation is free.
  • Keywords: partial evaluation, Futumura projections, weight-space programming, recursive self-improvement, bespoke software
  • Core insight: AI-driven partial evaluation turns code into a free, infinitely customizable commodity, making traditional software engineering, dependency management, and IP protection obsolete.

- **Evidence**: Comparison of the cost of generation versus monthly SaaS subscriptions.
- **Practical implication**: Companies selling generic software will face severe disruption and layoffs.
### Tokens scale, humans don't
- **Explanation**: Human productivity does not follow Moore's Law, but AI token processing power and capabilities scale rapidly.
- **Evidence**: Software engineering methodologies like Agile failed to make human coders exponentially more productive.
- **Practical implication**: Organizations must replace human bottlenecks with AI-driven generation and agents.
### LLMs achieve recursive self-improvement via partial evaluation
- **Explanation**: Partial evaluation allows AI systems to optimize code and neural networks recursively without needing god-like understanding.
- **Evidence**: Recent MIT papers on 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming'.
- **Practical implication**: AI will systematically optimize its own models and software infrastructure.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Three Futumura Projections
- **How it works**: Taking a partial evaluator (mix) and feeding interpreters and itself into it to derive executables, compilers, and compiler generators.
- **Components**:
  - First Projection (Executable): mix(interpreter, program) -> executable
  - Second Projection (Compiler): mix(mix, interpreter) -> compiler
  - Third Projection (Generator): mix(mix, mix) -> compiler generator
- **When to use**: When optimizing program execution and understanding program specialization.
### Three Ways to Specialize a Model
- **How it works**: Methods to adapt a general-purpose model to specific tasks.
- **Components**:
  - Partial Evaluation
  - Fine-Tuning
  - Distillation
- **When to use**: When tailoring large models for efficient, specialized deployment.
## Examples & Case Studies
### PostgreSQL 19 release delays attributed to AI finding bugs in human-written code faster than humans can ship.
- **Illustrates**: Human software is full of bugs, and AI is exposing the flaws in human coding standards.
- **Lesson**: Human-written software is inherently buggy; AI verification will become mandatory.
### Specializing a neural network (MNIST) to recognize only digits 0 through 4.
- **Illustrates**: Partial evaluation applied to neural network weights (weight-space programming).
- **Lesson**: Models can be drastically reduced in size and improved in accuracy without retraining by evaluating known static inputs.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Stop relying on bloated open-source dependency trees; use AI to statically link and generate custom applications.
  - Embrace partial evaluation concepts in prompt engineering and model optimization.
- **Strategic**:
  - Shift business models from selling software licenses to selling outcomes and services built with AI.
  - Prepare for recursive self-improvement in AI systems by 2027.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How will enterprise architectures adapt to zero-dependency, AI-generated micro-applications?
  - What are the legal and practical limits of weight-space programming and model distillation?

## Compressed Summary
- Software is transitioning from generic and expensive to custom and cheap via AI partial evaluation.
- Futumura projections explain how interpreters, compilers, and code generators relate mathematically.
- LLMs act as partial evaluators, enabling weight-space programming and recursive self-improvement.
- Software IP, patents, and copyright are increasingly irrelevant because code generation is free.
- **Keywords**: partial evaluation, Futumura projections, weight-space programming, recursive self-improvement, bespoke software
- **Core insight**: AI-driven partial evaluation turns code into a free, infinitely customizable commodity, making traditional software engineering, dependency management, and IP protection obsolete.
